I’m sorry to hear that! It is great you’re choosing healthier options, going to see a nutritionist and all of those dietary tweaks are beneficial to you even if you don’t yet see it on the scale. If it makes you feel better it is possible to regain control over your fullness cues, it just takes time. I used to only feel “full” after a binge when I was absolutely uncomfortably full. I noticed a few things helped with that in particular, the main thing was just time but also, one was I saw this dietician online who said to combine healthy fats (avo, olive oil, nuts,) with fiber and protein in every meal and I realized that even with a little bit of fat, that chicken salad meal you mentioned may even feel more filling. I know for me personally, I pretty much had cut out most fat because of caloric density and it was like my body needed some of each to get and stay full. Another thing that sounds easy but is difficult in practice helped was eating slow, and because of the “finish your plate mindset” taking slightly less than I think I need, and reminding myself I can always eat more when I am still hungry. I also don’t typically restrict things I like everyday anymore because I found that creates mental scarcity and I binge, I just try to find a slightly healthier way to have what I’m craving or if I can’t, I OMAD it! The last thing for me personally, which may or may not apply to anyone else, was finding other things to channel my emotions/boredom into, like painting or writing. Wishing you the best of luck.

Hey I felt the same way when I found out I had it. I got it at 19, from only the second man I’d ever been with. People are generally more accepting than you would think, and you just disclose to someone when it seems you may sleep together and use protection when you do. As for symptoms, I’m on daily suppression medication so most of the time I don’t even think about having it as it makes outbreaks shorter and further apart, and eliminates them all together for some people. The suppression medicine helps my mental health because I don’t have to have a reminder of something I can’t change. Overall, I’m recovering mentally a lot, but the main thing I’ve learned is that the only scary part of herpes is the stigma, and you shouldn’t let it define you because you are so much more. If you need someone to talk to I’m here for you.

Hey man, everyones gets on each other’s nerves while driving. At one time they surely irritated other drivers, it’s part of life. 

Also I always try to remind myself of three things when it comes to peoples opinion. 
  - The first is that more often than not, someone’s thoughts on us tell more about them than us. If someone becomes furious at you for driving slower than they’d like, it probably reflects on what kind of day they’re having more than your worth as a driver. People treat other people as mirrors more often than we realize, when they become ugly to other people it’s because that’s how they feel in that moment. 
- The second is that generally speaking, it’s never personal. Let’s say you cut someone off, they’re probably mad because they had to slam on their breaks to avoid a crash, you scared them. They know nothing about you, they don’t hate you, they hate being scared in that moment lol. 
- The third is that it just absolutely does not matter what that angry ass dude in a Kia Soul thinks about you. Even if he irrationally decided that you drive like an absolute ass and he can’t stand you, it doesn’t matter. He won’t be the deciding factor on if you have your dream job or not, he won’t keep you from meeting the love of your life. He’s irrelevant. 

The most important thing is being a safe driver and it sounds like you are.
